title: us japan yen team up worsens boj dilemma 2026 08 03
author: Hudson Lockett
text:
HONG KONG, Aug 3 (Reuters Breakingviews) - The goal of the latest yen intervention is a riddle, wrapped in a mystery, inside an enigma. Following a coordinated action by the U.S. and Japan, the currency’s dollar ​exchange rate stands more than 4% firmer. But the underlying drivers of weakness remain, raising the question of what the ‌push hopes to achieve in the longer term. Growing pressure for coordination with the Bank of Japan may have a more lasting impact, and for the worse.
The Japanese finance ministry confirmed the joint action on Monday after central bank data showed the government may have sold as much as $59 billion of securities on Thursday to support its currency. On ​Friday, the Financial Times
, opens new tab
, citing unnamed sources, reported that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York had sold euros to buy yen ​on behalf of the U.S. Treasury. That same day a Reuters photo revealed Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s “to-do” list at a ⁠cabinet meeting: “Buy Japanese Yen (JPY) $5-10 bil”.
All this is necessary because of Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s desire to turbocharge growth via a 370 trillion yen ($2.4 trillion) investment ​splurge, funded by government bond sales that will sink the country’s currency. She also wants to cut a food-sales tax, leaving a budgetary shortfall requiring ​more debt issuance to offset. With no sign of the prime minister backing down from either ambition, pressure has mounted on the Bank of Japan to raise rates more quickly to offset yen weakness. But Takaichi has expressed a preference for loose monetary policy to enable government spending — one of her recent appointees to the central bank’s ​board was the sole dissent in June’s 7-1 vote to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points to 1%.
Enter Bessent once more. In a post
, opens new tab
 to ​X on Friday, he lauded Takaichi, BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda and the central bank's board. He also took pains to mention plans to meet with Ueda later ‌this month ⁠while talking up the two countries' "strong relationship and close coordination".
The glass-half-full interpretation is that the U.S. supports the BOJ in raising rates further, but this carries the downside of suggesting that Japanese interest rates are ultimately being set by Washington. If Ueda and his fellow board members decide – with good reason – to hike again in September after he meets with Bessent, it could undermine perceptions of central bank independence instead of boosting them. It’s exactly ​the sort of monetary policy nightmare ​every central banker hopes to ⁠avoid.
